books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, C. A Temporary Truce on the Slavery Question in the Pre-Civil War Period

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the House of Representatives’ gag rule, first adopted in 1836: Any petition or resolution about slavery would be laid on the table without being read, printed, or debated. The rule stayed in force until 1844. Former president John Quincy Adams, then a member of the House from Massachusetts, fought the rule in every session.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the House gag resolutions (Pinckney resolutions), 1836-1844, as described in Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.3 C, and Princeton Review 25e, Chapter 8, 'The Abolition Movement.'

source: original; stimulus paraphrases the House gag rule, 1836-1844, from the grounding books
stem: Under the House gag rule, an antislavery petition sent to Congress would be

options.text: read aloud and put to a vote the same day
options.misconception: The rule did the opposite: petitions were tabled without being read.

options.text: laid on the table without being read or debated
sent to the Senate for a hearing
options.misconception: The gag rule kept petitions in the House, tabled; it sent nothing to the Senate.

options.text: published in the Congressional Record as a law
options.misconception: A petition is a request, not a law; the rule kept it from even being read.

rationales.A: Read aloud and voted on is exactly what the rule prevented. Tabled means set aside, unread.
rationales.B: The rule said every slavery petition would be laid on the table, unread, unprinted, undebated. That is the gag in the gag rule.
rationales.C: The rule was a House rule about House business. It did not move petitions to the Senate; it buried them in the House.
rationales.D: Petitions do not become laws, and this rule kept them from being published or read at all.
rationales.general:
1. Read the rule. Petitions about slavery are laid on the table without being read, printed, or debated.
2. Ask what “laid on the table” means. Set aside, not acted on.
3. Check the other choices. A vote, a Senate hearing, and a published law all require the petition to be heard.
4. Put it together. The rule’s whole point was that the petition would not be heard.
Remember: a rule’s name often states its effect, so read the name first.
